extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, taxonomists, and students of natural history/evolutionary biology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for classifying organisms and judging affinities based on descent, morphology, embryology, geography, and patterns of variation under natural selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of correlated/aggregated characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Correlated or aggregated characters have especial value in classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple characters, even if individually trifling, taken together across a large group provide strong evidence of common parentage. Prefer aggregated character sets over single isolated characters when inferring relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of number of characters for inferring descent
rubrics_metrics.description: A sufficient number of characters, let them be ever so unimportant, betrays the hidden bond of community of descent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if two extreme forms share no single character, if they are connected by intermediate groups with shared characters, group them together. Emphasize the cumulative signal of many small characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight given to organs of high physiological importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Organs of high physiological importance — those which serve to preserve life under diverse conditions — are generally the most constant and are of especial value in classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give greater classificatory weight to stable, life-preserving structures; if such organs differ greatly between groups, down-weight their importance in that comparative context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-dependent valuation of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: We value certain resemblances far more than others; a character may be valuable within a group but not between groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same character can be a true affinity within a class/order but analogical between classes (e.g., fin-like limbs in cetaceans vs fishes). Always assess characters relative to the taxonomic scale of comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: High classificatory importance of embryological characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Embryological characters are of such high classificatory importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarity of embryonic stages among species within a class provides strong evidence of common descent (Agassiz anecdote: indistinguishable vertebrate embryos). Use embryology especially where adult characters are divergent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of geographical distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical distribution may sometimes be usefully brought into play in classing large and widely-distributed genera.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Species of the same genus inhabiting a distinct and isolated region have in all probability descended from the same parents. Use geography as supporting evidence for common descent, especially for large genera with regional endemism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between real affinities and analogical/adaptive resemblances
rubrics_metrics.description: Real affinities reveal descent; analogical or adaptive resemblances do not and are almost valueless to the systematist when comparing distinct lines of descent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject adaptive similarities that arise from similar environmental pressures (e.g., dugong/whale/fish body shape) when inferring genealogical relationships. Look for non-adaptive, correlated characters indicating inheritance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of adaptive characters within groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Adaptive (analogical) characters may be used within the limits of the same group but are to be summarily rejected when comparing distinct groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within a family or order, adaptive characters can still indicate affinity because they are combined with many other shared characters; between higher taxa, beware of convergence obscuring true relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about numerical parallelism in classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical parallelism (septenary, quinary, etc.) in classifications has probably arisen from arbitrary valuation and should be viewed with caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not force taxa into numerically neat schemes; valuation of group ranks has been arbitrary and can be manipulated to create apparent parallels across classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of dominance and size of groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Modified descendants of dominant species (larger genera) tend to inherit advantages that make groups large and dominant; larger groups tend to spread and supplant smaller groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the disproportionate size and widespread nature of a few great orders/classes by historical processes of descent and selection rather than special creation; use group size and spread as contextual evidence for past success and radiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of aberrant/osculant groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Aberrant or osculant groups are those in which ancient intermediate parent-forms transmitted little-modified descendants, and such groups are often represented by very few and distinct species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rare, highly distinct genera (e.g., Ornithorhynchus, Lepidosiren) likely indicate extinction of many connecting forms; treat such aberrant taxa as failed or relict lineages when reconstructing affinities.

rubrics_metrics.name: General (not special) affinities indicate deep common ancestry
rubrics_metrics.description: When a member of one group exhibits an affinity to a quite distinct group, the affinity is usually general (not to a single species) and implies inheritance from an ancient common progenitor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If resemblance is widespread across a target group rather than specifically to one species, interpret as shared retention of ancestral characters rather than recent convergence. Use examples like bizcacha vs marsupials to distinguish patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of descent as the hidden bond of the Natural System
rubrics_metrics.description: Descent (genealogical arrangement) is the hidden bond which naturalists have sought under the term of the Natural System.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify by lines of descent: use genealogy to group sexes, ages, varieties and species, and to define genera, families and orders. Prefer genealogical reasoning over appeals to a creation plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology and unity of type as evidence of affinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Homologous structures (unity of type) — the same pattern of organisation across species — indicate common descent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize relative connexion and order of parts (e.g., same bones in mammal limbs). Homology is stronger evidence than mere functional similarity; use common patterns even when functions differ widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serial (within-individual) homology
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison of different parts/organs in the same individual (serial homology) can reveal common elements (e.g., skull bones and vertebræ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use serial homologies to understand morphological transformations and to infer deeper structural commonality; consider that parts may be metamorphosed from a common element rather than from one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of repetition of parts for variation and modification
rubrics_metrics.description: An indefinite repetition of the same part or organ in ancestral forms predisposes those elements to vary in number and structure and be seized upon by natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that repeated elements (vertebræ, segments, whorls of leaves) are sources of morphological innovation; this explains why limbs, mouthparts, and floral organs diversify yet retain a common pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embryonic similarity as non-adaptive evidence of affinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Embryos of distinct animals within the same class are often strikingly similar, and these resemblances frequently have no direct relation to conditions of existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat conserved embryonic structures as strong evidence of common ancestry because they are less likely to be adaptive for diverse early-life conditions; exceptions occur when embryos/larvæ are active and independently adapted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat: active larval/embryonic adaptation can obscure affinities
rubrics_metrics.description: When an embryo or larva is active and must provide for itself, its adaptations can obscure embryonic resemblance to relatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-rely on embryology in taxa with strongly adapted larval stages (e.g., active insect larvæ); assess lifecycle ecology to know when embryonic characters are reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of variation expression (age-correspondence principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations tend to reappear at a corresponding age in the offspring as in the parent; the period when variation is displayed matters for classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ontogenetic timing: if characteristic differences manifest late in life, young stages of allied species will resemble each other more than adults (domestic pigeons/dogs/horses examples). Consider both possibilities where exceptions occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of types when groups blend
rubrics_metrics.description: When continuous gradations exist, pick out types representing most characters of each group to give a general idea of differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases where groups cannot be sharply defined due to fine gradations, select representative types to communicate the value of differences; recognize limits of rigid definitions when all forms could be reassembled.
